result:
Both integrate changes from one branch into another; they differ in what they do to history.

**Merge** ties the two histories together with a new merge commit. Existing commits are untouched.

```
A---B---C---M   main
     \     /
      D---E     feature
```

**Rebase** replays your commits on top of the other branch, creating new commits with new hashes. History becomes linear, as if you'd started your work from the latest tip.

```
A---B---C---D'---E'   feature (rebased onto main)
```

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves what actually happened, branches and all | Linear, rewritten |
| Commits | Adds a merge commit | Recreates your commits (new hashes) |
| Conflicts | Resolved once, in the merge commit | Resolved per replayed commit |
| Safe on shared branches | Yes | No, it rewrites history others may have based work on |
| Undo | Revert the merge commit | `git reflog` to find the old tip |

**Rule of thumb:**
- Rebase your own local, unpushed work to tidy it up or catch up with `main` (`git rebase main`).
- Merge when integrating into a shared branch, or when the branch is already pushed and others use it.
- Never rebase commits other people have pulled. If you rebased a branch you had already pushed, you'll need `git push --force-with-lease`, which is only fine if the branch is yours alone.
